records.query: Explain the components and design of the AFTF.
records.reference: The AFTF (Aircraft Fire Training Facility) is a fixed site simulator for realistic aircraft fire suppression training. It includes a 100-foot burn area, an aircraft mock-up with water-cooled jackets and ignitors, a water pond, and a 10,000-gallon tank for water recycling. The fuel system uses liquid propane (LPG) to simulate multiple fire types, including airframe, engine, and ground fires. The facility is managed via a safety/control stand with electrical, pneumatic, and water systems, and is equipped with manual/pneumatic shutoff valves, an E-stop switch, and fuel shutoff valves for JP-8 and propane for emergency control.

Training fills the burn area with water to one inch (2.54 cm) above the aggregate level, supplies propane through underground pipes, and ignites fuel using 10,000 volt, 23 milliampere ignitors located in 15 burners, controlled by switches and valves on the control stand. The AFTF consists of an aircraft mock-up, burn area, control stand, compressor shelter, and integrated systems: liquid propane fuel, cathodic (anti-corrosion) protection, pneumatic system, electrical system, and a water conservation system with a holding pond incorporating submerged and aeration pumps with an associated sprinkler, water jackets, drain and wash down systems. The aircraft mock-up sits in the burn area with an underground liner, is constructed of uncoated/unpainted carbon steel, is approximately 72 feet long, 25 feet high at tail tip, with a 72-foot wingspan. It has four simulated engines (two on the right high wing, one on the vertical stabilizer, and one forward of the left wing known as the Engine Debris trainer), each with a burner assembly and two ignitors; ignitor wiring is enclosed in water jackets. Water injection is in both wing engines and at some sites in the tail engine; wing engines have dams and plumbing for running fuel fires; wheel well and APU fires are simulated on the high wing side adjacent to the inboard engine; the outboard engine has plumbing for a large running fuel fire with ground pool and spill fires below. Interior ignitors and burners simulate cockpit, passenger compartment, and cargo fires. A water sprinkler system along the fuselage top cools and washes down the mock-up, with water circulated from the burn area to the environmental pond and back via drains and pumps. An expansion joint midway on the fuselage allows for expansion and contraction. Replaceable cutout panels (0.031 inch sheet metal) on both sides simulate emergency entry, and steel hinged doors are on the left and right sides, with the rear left troop door configured as the Pyrolance trainer. Consumable items (solenoids, regulators, valves, switches, and ignitors) must be discarded upon disassembly unless manufacturer-authorized rebuild/repair kits are available.

records.query: Summarize the procedures and safety requirements for removing, packaging, and handling wet and dry batteries from vehicles; mention hazard precautions as well.
records.reference: Wet batteries (except nickel, iron-alkaline) must be removed from vehicles and reported as excess, kept charged, and maintained in a charged condition while awaiting disposal instructions. Dry batteries should be space packaged and packed in accordance with Specification PPP-B-140, with vent holes sealed. Battery posts must be protected using plastic caps or tape conforming to Specification SAE AMS-T-22085. Wet batteries may remain installed in vehicles during military aircraft transport if protected against short circuits by disconnecting and securing cables away from terminals, and properly secured to prevent acid leakage. Dry batteries pose no special hazard and may be installed in the vehicle or shipped with OVE without additional precautions. Wet batteries received with vehicles may be used until the first exercise is completed, after which they must be transferred to a battery room, kept charged, and either shipped or replaced with dry batteries. Dry batteries, whether received charged or not, can be stored in the vehicle’s battery carrier, though indoor storage is preferred, and their vent holes must be sealed until activation. Cable terminals should be greased and taped according to military specifications, and dry batteries must not be activated unless no serviceable wet battery is available. Hazard precautions include preventing acid leakage and short circuits for wet batteries, and ensuring proper handling and activation procedures for dry batteries to avoid chemical exposure.

records.query: What are the procedures for installing, removing, and requisitioning vehicle markings, including reflective tape?
records.reference: Vehicle markings, including reflective tape, are installed by cleaning the surface, removing the liner, positioning the tape, and applying firm pressure. For removal, pressure-sensitive tape can be softened with heat and isopropyl alcohol (TT-I-735), while older tape requires paint remover (TT-R-2918) or 3M decal remover disks. Markings can be requisitioned through DLA Document Services Online. If decals are unavailable and safety is impacted, stenciling is permitted. Reflectors follow drawing B161059, mounted 24–60 inches above the ground, visible at 100 feet. Install tape according to the steps; damaged areas may be patched.
records.answer:
Installation of reflectorized tape (P5240, para 2.88): (a) clean the vehicle surface before applying the marking; (b) remove the liner film down; (c) position the emblem on the clean surface and tack it in place with thumb pressure; (d) start in the center using hard overlapping strokes of low friction plastic squeeze; (e) re-squeeze the edges using very firm strokes; (f) apply clean sealer to the edges of the tape; (g) repairs to damaged areas can be made without stripping the original tape by cleaning the damaged area and applying new tape over the affected area.

Removal of reflectorized tape (P5240 WARNING; P5241): WARNING: Lacquer thinner, kylol, and isopropyl alcohol are flammable and toxic. Good general ventilation is normally adequate. Skin and eye protection is required. Avoid all sources of ignition. Failure to comply could result in injury to, or death of, personnel or long term health hazards. Routine removal (2.89.1): soften pressure sensitive tape with heat (heat lamp, heat gun, steam, etc.); soften adhesive residue with rags soaked in ISOPROPYL ALCOHOL, TT-1-735, and scrape away with plastic scraper or putty knife. Removing old tape (2.89.2): mask off the area, brush PAINT REMOVER, TT-R-2918, Type over the tape, possibly several applications at short intervals, removing residue with plastic scraper or bevel edge putty knife between applications; the remover may damage the paint beneath, requiring cleaning and touchup painting. Alternative (2.89.3): use a 4 or 6 inch stripe, molding and decal remover disk (3M), NSN 5130-01-390-9503 (4 inches) or NSN 5130-01-390-9504 (6 inches), with adapter NSN 5130-01-391-2095 for use with a drill; solvents are flammable and toxic, so all safety precautions apply.

Requisitioning of markings (2.90, P5241): all markings in the chapter can be requisitioned through DLA Document Services via the Document Services Online (DSO) website; after an account is created, orders are processed through the Travis Plant. DLA Document Services contact: (707) 424-0770/(707) 424-4537, DSN 837. NOTE: If decals are not available on immediate requisition and the equipment hampers mission capability or presents a safety hazard unmarked, appropriate markings may be stenciled on vehicles or equipment before decals are received.

records.query: What caution is taken into consideration while using high-pressure wash equipment, and explain the function of the portable, 45-gallon, foam-generating cleaning unit?
records.reference: When using high-pressure wash equipment, caution must be taken to ensure it is never used on aircraft landing gear and components, wheels, and brakes, as it can force lubricants out of bearings and attachment points, causing corrosion and wear problems. The function of the portable, 45-gallon, foam-generating cleaning unit is to dispense foam. This cleaning unit is a simplified, portable, pressure-operated, foam-dispensing system that uses the available air supply as its power source to force cleaning solution into the hose and create foam.
records.answer: CAUTION (P3208): Do not use high pressure spray nozzles to apply cleaning compounds; cleaning compounds shall only be applied using a low pressure soap nozzle, because high pressure can cause cleaning compounds to become entrapped in enclosed areas causing corrosion. records.query: Define CSO and list down the activities performed in the presence of CSS.
records.reference: Concurrent Servicing Operations (CSO) are the simultaneous servicing of fuel and other aircraft operations such as munitions loading/unloading, aircraft reconfiguration, and aircraft -6 TO inspections. The Chief Servicing Supervisor (CSS) is responsible for on-site supervision of all aspects of concurrent fuel servicing operations. The CSS's activities include ensuring all non-essential personnel and equipment are cleared from the area, briefing team members on duties and emergency procedures, checking the status of the aircraft and its systems with the SCR, ensuring cabin crew have briefed passengers, directing and monitoring the positioning of support equipment and personnel, and having SPR/Vent monitors reposition aircraft wheel chocks as required.
records.answer: CSO (Concurrent Servicing Operations) supporting Combat Sortie Generation (CSG) is defined as the simultaneous fueling and munitions/ammunition loading/unloading, aircraft reconfiguration, aircraft -6 TO inspections, and other aircraft servicing such as oil, nitrogen, and hydraulic fluid; oxygen servicing will not be accomplished during fuel servicing. Activities performed under the CSS, per the pages provided: (1) Meeting with the SCR to determine status of the aircraft and its systems, and verifying fuel jettison valves are closed before fuel servicing starts; (2) Ensuring cabin crew briefs passengers on fuel servicing; (3) Directing positioning of support equipment at the aircraft, including the air conditioner (outside the FSSZ), lavatory and portable water trucks, and hydrant hose cart(s) or refueling vehicles; (4) Informing refueling team members the aircraft is ready for refueling; (5) Requesting the REO to start fuel flow; (6) Monitoring the wing fuel vent on the opposite side from the SPR (SPR/fuel vent monitors and WVM as applicable); (7) Ensuring assistance to the REO in wrapping and storing refueling hoses, removing grounding/bonding wires, and clearing equipment from the area; (8) Having the LVM reposition wheel chocks as required; (9) Removing equipment no longer required from the concurrent servicing area; (10) Releasing refueling team members; (11) Maintaining constant voice contact via intercom with cockpit personnel, SPR/fuel vent monitors, and the fuel control panel operator; (12) Stopping fuel flow in an emergency. Warning: stop refueling if fuel flow does not stop during precheck until corrected. Caution: do not exceed 55 PSI refueling pressure at the refueling source (for L-188, do not exceed 300 GPM at 35 PSI maximum).
